I found Hormozi's own notes on this in the vault, and he says it directly in two videos. Here's the answer.

**Verdict:** Yes. Admit your flaws, and put them up front. Hormozi calls admitting your weaknesses ("damaging admissions") possibly his favorite tactic: "nothing more powerful than damaging admissions." You give up a little promise and gain trust, and to him trust wins.

**Based on:** he said it directly, in two videos about a year apart (May 2025 and Feb 2026). His view didn't change between them.

**Why he'd say it**
- Every product has flaws, so say them: "you want to always own your flaws of course you have them of course your product isn't perfect say so" ([video, 12:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=750s)).
- Trust beats a bigger claim: "what you'll sacrifice in promise you'll gain in trust and trust trumps promise … I would rather always sacrifice promise to gain trust" ([13:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=789s)).
- It makes you stand out: "if you want to stand out in a crowded marketplace tell the truth" ([15:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=939s)), because "what people won't say is the truth" ([16:15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=975s)).

**How to word it (his method)**
1. **List your flaws.** "write down all of the flaws all the things that people complain about the things that you know you could do better and claim them" ([15:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=903s)). Don't pick only the harmless ones. The aim is "to address all of the concerns they have upfront" ([13:44](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=824s)).
2. **Use "[true flaw], *but* [what you want them to believe]."** People remember what comes after "but": "the statement that comes after the word but is the part that is the thing you want them to believe" ([13:44](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=824s)). His own example: "our websites are ugly as hell but they convert" ([15:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=903s)).
   - Never reverse the order. "It converts, but it's ugly" leaves people thinking about the flaw.
3. **Make it funny if you can.** "if you can do with humor you get even more bonus points" ([15:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=939s)).
4. **Do the same on sales calls.** He has reps open with: "Listen, before I tell you about the good, let me tell you about the bad" ([second video, 19:42](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MH-IMJxbUY4&t=1182s)). Prospects who don't fit then rule themselves out: "So then they can self-qualify" ([20:14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MH-IMJxbUY4&t=1214s)). He says this matters most when an offer sounds too good to be true.

Some made-up examples of the pattern (these are mine, not his):
- "We're not the cheapest. But you'll only buy this once."
- "Setup takes an afternoon. But after that it runs itself."
- "Our app looks like it's from 2012. But it's the only one that does X."

**What would change his answer:** The vault doesn't record any exception. The method assumes two things, though: the flaw has to be true, and the claim after "but" has to hold up. If the flaw is serious enough to break the product's main promise, the problem is the offer, not the ad copy.

The research on admitting bias that he mentions, and his Eminem rap-battle story, are illustrations he cites, not his own data.

**Verdict:** Hormozi would say about 20% monthly churn is average for a paid online community, under 10% is best-in-class, and once more than 3 in 10 members leave each month, fixing retention is the most important thing you can work on. Before you worry about the average, though, look at when people leave. Churn should be high in months 1–3 and then drop sharply. If it doesn't, that's the real problem.

**Based on:** said it. This comes from one source, his 2026-03-24 retention talk "How to Get Your Customers to Stay FOREVER" (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q), and the numbers are Skool platform averages.

**The benchmarks**
- "the platform average across School is 80% monthly retention. So said differently, it's 20% churn… Now the best groups have less than 10% churn, aka 90% retention month over month. The not good groups have less than 70% retention, aka 30% or higher." ([@ 1:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=99s))
- When to worry: "if less than seven out of 10 people want to stay on a monthly basis, you probably need to work on your retention more than anything else. It'll be the highest ROI lever." (@ 1:39)
- Why it matters: cutting churn from 20% to 10% means "you didn't just get a 10 or 12% boost, you got a double in the LTV per customer" ([@ 2:13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=133s)).

**How churn changes with time**
- "the biggest rule is that churn drops dramatically with time" ([@ 3:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=199s)). After day 90 "it drops to around 10% or less", and by month six "it goes from like 10% to 2%" ([@ 3:53](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=233s)).
- So he changes the question from "How do I make this number go down?" to "How do I get someone to stay past day 90? How do I get these people to stay past month six?" ([@ 4:24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=264s))
- "don't overhaul your entire business because your month one churn sucks" (@ 4:24). Instead, he says to have a specific plan for getting people through month one.
- What gets people past each point: "Day 90 is probably going to have to deliver some sort of outcome… Month six, it's usually them connecting with other people within that community." ([@ 5:31](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=331s))

**When to worry, in his terms**
1. Each month, track how many people joined and how many cancelled, and call the business growing, flat or declining based on that (@ 0:33).
2. Worry if monthly retention is below 70%. Then retention comes before everything else, including getting more members.
3. Worry if long-time members keep leaving. Losing people after month 3, and especially after month 6, means the community isn't delivering results or connecting members to each other.
4. Don't panic about a new community. One under 90 days old, or under 6 months, will look worse than it is because nobody has reached the low-churn months yet.

**What he'd tell you to do about it**
- Cut overwhelm, which he calls "the number one reason people churn, outside of price" ([@ 9:18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=558s)).
- Show up in the community every day. Owners who did had "significantly higher retention" ([@ 13:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=819s)).
- Run one big thing per week, like a live call.
- Get each new member "one real friend" and introduce them to about 10 regulars.

**What would change his answer:** He says these numbers fit online and consumer services, not things like insurance or alarm systems. A cheap or very low-commitment community may naturally sit closer to the average, and an annual plan would make monthly churn numbers misleading.

One thing to keep in mind: all of these numbers come from Skool, a platform Hormozi is involved with, and from a single talk. They're a useful benchmark, not an industry-wide figure.

**Verdict:** Pay it off within a few months. Don't stop spending on growth that already has proven returns while you do it. Hormozi was asked almost exactly your question, about a profitable service business with $60k of debt. He approved the owner's plan to clear it in four to five months, put debt paydown second on the priority list, and in the same list told him to raise ad spend.

**Based on:** he said it (confidence: high). The case in the vault is close to yours: Corey, an HVAC-cleaning company owner with $1.25M in revenue, a 38% net margin and $60k of debt.
Source: *Building a $2,500,000 Business for a Stranger in 36 Minutes* (2026-05-08), https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4

**Why he'd say it**
- He leans toward Dave Ramsey: "I tend to skew like very close to the Ramsey side" ([@ 8:37](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=517s)).
- His one argument is that debt adds risk, and over enough time that risk shows up: "Risk when multiplied over a long time horizon tends to come due." Also: "businesses have seasons, they have volatility" ([@ 9:10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=550s)).
- He points to debt-free companies that have lasted: "If you look at some of the most enduring companies, a lot of like Chick-fil-A operate debt free." (@ 9:10)
- He admits part of the reason is psychological rather than a big financial lever: "I'd say this is more of an emotional thing, but it's just this back of mind thing." (@ 8:37)
- It fits a wider rule of his: get safe first so you can take risks later. "you get rewarded for the risk you take on. You cannot take any risk on if you have no time and no money." (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk&t=784s)

**Why "pay it off" doesn't mean "stop growing"**
He doesn't treat this as a choice between the two. The plan he wrote for Corey ([@ 30:45](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=1845s)) was, in order:
1. Raise prices 10%.
2. "continue to pay off the debt."
3. Fix the funnel.
4. Fix the ads, then increase ad spend.

On spending with proven returns he's aggressive. Corey's ads were already returning about 13:1, and Hormozi said: "if you know that's where the money's coming from, by all means, spend more" ([@ 11:21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=681s)). He called that kind of spending "part of leveling up in business is that you take greater and greater risk, and at the same time, you get greater and greater rewards" (@ 11:54).

So by his logic you'd do both:
- Pay the debt down fast out of profit.
- Fund the growth channels you've already proven, starting with the cheap ones like a price increase and fixing the funnel.
- Don't keep the debt around as a cushion for growth bets you haven't tested.

**What would change his answer:** He asks why the debt was taken on ("cuz I wanted to grow faster"), but he never says when borrowing to grow is justified. Elsewhere he describes heavy leverage as how private-equity fund managers get "mega rich," and he doesn't reconcile that with his Ramsey lean. If your debt is cheap and paying it off would starve a channel with proven returns, his "spend more on proven ROI" rule could take priority. That's my inference; he hasn't said it.

My own view: with 13:1-type returns available, the math clearly favors spending first. But his advice is to do both at once, and with profit like yours that's usually possible.

**Verdict:** No, he'd tell you to raise prices about 10%. In his view an 82% close rate means you're underpriced, and the raise pays off as long as you keep closing more than 65%.

**Based on:** said it. He was asked almost exactly this. Your numbers match an episode with Corey, who owns Proshine, an HVAC duct-cleaning company: $1.25M trailing 12 months, 38% net margin, 82% close rate. ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4), May 2026)

**What he said**
- **The close-rate rule:** "So whenever I hear 80% or over 80% close rates, I usually know that there's room in sale." (@ [8:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=486s))
- **The break-even:** "We would have to believe that we're not going to drop to 65%. As long as we close more than 65%, we make more money." (@ 8:06) The math checks out for your margin. A 10% raise lifts profit per job from 38% to about 48% of the old price, so you can lose about 21% of your jobs and still break even. 82% × 0.79 ≈ 65%.
- **The upside:** "that 10% price raise for you equals roughly a 25% increase in net profit." (@ 8:06) He put that at "roughly a hundred plus thousand a year" at the previous year's volume (@ [8:37](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=517s)). The specific plan was about $1,650 per unit, up from $1,575 (@ 30:45).
- **Why it might not hurt your close rate at all:** for an ordinary service, a higher price makes customers more confident you can deliver. "if you raise your prices, what sometimes happens is that the conviction of the customer that you can actually deliver on the promise you're making goes up." (@ [7:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=420s)) A price that's too low makes you look like a "super seedy duct tape operation" (@ 7:33).
- **Who he says it applies to:** owners under about $3–5M in revenue. "some of the biggest levers that exist in the business is simply charging more" (@ 8:06)

**What he's done:** Corey had already raised prices 23% after an earlier Acquisition.com workshop, and that "resulted in a higher close rate and more money" (@ 5:54–6:26). The 10% raise was the next step on top of that. A year later Corey was on track for $2.3–2.5M. In the check-in, though, Corey credits mostly marketing and lead flow (about 120 → 200 leads a month), not pricing on its own.

**What would change his answer**
- **If your close rate falls below about 65% after the raise:** that's his own condition. He called the 10% "more asking than telling" (@ 8:06), so treat it as a test and watch the close rate.
- **If you've already raised prices recently:** Corey's 23% raise came first. If you've done the same, you're in his exact spot and another 10% is the move. If you haven't, he'd probably say you have even more room.
- **Your competitors' prices:** his first raise came from comparing prices across that space and concluding Corey was "mispriced" (@ 6:26). Check where you sit against local competitors.

Related ideas from the vault you could add on top: offer a much more expensive premium tier as a price anchor, and charge a priority fee for faster scheduling when demand is higher than your crews can handle ("speed's all margin").

I found the passage. The main finding is that Hormozi isn't the one who tells this story.

**Verdict:** It's Steven Bartlett's story, not Hormozi's. It comes from *The Diary Of A CEO* E235 (2023-04-03), where Bartlett is the host and tells it to Hormozi. Hormozi's part is the response, and that's where his own view shows up.

**Based on:** said it (raw transcript, auto-captions; this part of the episode isn't in the wiki yet)

**The story (Bartlett speaking)**
- His company (Social Chain) listed on a European exchange. While they were considering another IPO, investment banks on the roadshow told him: "if you move it to the NASDAQ the exact same business would be worth four times more" ([1:34:12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=5652s)).
- He took the lesson to be that you need to know which market to apply a skill to, not just have the skill. He decided his social media and storytelling skills were worth the most to companies about to IPO, because "if you have a good story it can swing your valuation by hundreds of millions" (1:35:17).
- The equity deal: he did 9 to 12 months of what he calls "basically freelance" work for a company before its IPO, which listed at about $3B. On IPO day his equity was "worth in the region of 7 to8 million" (1:35:51). That's why he started Flight Story, which began in the IPO market (1:36:23).

**Hormozi's response**
- He agrees and frames it as fishing where the fish are: "same work yeah same amount of time same Rod more zeros" ([1:38:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=5883s)).
- He gives his own conversion-rate example. A 20% lift for a $1M store earns you about $20K. The same lift for a $100M business earns you about $2M: "20,000 2 million 100x same work." He links this to his tweet "solve rich people problems they pay better" (1:38:38). This is the "sell to better customers" idea from his first book.
- Later he uses the NASDAQ point as an example of capital leverage. Friends-and-family money comes first, then institutional money, then public money: "the fact that the NASDAQ was Forex uh the dorf exchange... there's just significantly more capital in that" ([1:45:47](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=6347s)). ("Forex" is how the auto-captions render "4x".)

**What Hormozi has done:** Nothing in this passage. The IPO equity deal and the 4x valuation gap both happened to Bartlett.

This section of the episode isn't in the wiki yet. If you want it cited properly, I can add Hormozi's "same work, more zeros" and "solve rich people problems" quotes to the premium-pricing leaf.

**Correction: he didn't tell him that. He told him the opposite.** In the vault's only roofing consult (Caleb, Keys Roofing, St. Louis: a two-month-old business doing about $20K a month from door-knocking and referrals), Hormozi said to **go all in on door-to-door** and build a team of reps to knock doors. He never told him to stop knocking, and he never recommended Google Ads. The only time "Google" comes up in that transcript is Caleb saying he asks customers for a Google review (@ 12:02).

**Based on:** said it. Source: "How I Would Build a $10M Service Business (If I Had to Start Over)", https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU

**What he actually said, and why**
- **Put everything into what already works.** "I want to focus all efforts on the highest return stuff that you can do right now." ([@ 3:16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU&t=196s))
- **Being able to close at the door is rare.** "that reliability of being able to just basically go get money um is something that a lot of entrepreneurs don't know how to do." (@ 3:16) He compares it to a cat's nine lives: an entrepreneur who knows how to go get money gets extra lives.
- **Don't get clever with new channels.** "Now I think that in terms of scale, you should go all in door to door." ([@ 9:49](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU&t=589s)) / "It's what you're good at." / "Like I don't think we need to be cute about this." ([@ 10:21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU&t=621s))
- **Grow it with a team, and pay reps per door.** "want to go make 10 bucks? Knock that door." / "I think you building out this DDD army is like the clear straight shot." ([@ 10:54](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU&t=654s)) "DDD" is the auto-caption's spelling of D2D, door-to-door. The $10 is his example: a 10% commission on a $4K repair, spread across about 50 doors per sale.
- **His recap at the end:** "the first thing we said was go all in on door to door as primary growth engine." ([@ 24:27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU&t=1467s))

**Rest of his advice in that consult:** raise the average repair ticket, use VSLs to answer objections before the sales call, add a maintenance membership, use a menu upsell, and charge extra for faster service. Caleb reported going from about $32K to about $247K by the 90-day check-in. Those are his own figures, and the video doesn't say whether they're monthly or cumulative.

**What would change his answer:** the reason he gave was that door-knocking was the channel Caleb already closed on, at about 1 sale per 20 doors. If door-knocking stopped producing sales, that reason would go away. But the vault has nothing from him saying Google Ads would be the replacement.

If you're thinking of a different video where he did say this, it isn't in the vault. Send me the link and I can add it.
